NRBS 3410 
Summer 2026
Historical Context 
Maternal Fetal Health

Historical Development: 
Maternal and Newborn Nursing
 Colonial America: childbirth was a difficult and 
dangerous experience
 Early 1900s: physician assisted births; midwives for 
those who could not afford a doctor
 1950s: introduction of natural childbirth practices 
 Current: return of midwives and doulas; childbirth 
choices based on what works best for mother, child, 
and family
 Only 12% of births in US were with Midwives
 32.1% of all US births are via cesarean section 
(2022 National Center Healthcare Statistics)

Maternal-Infant Statistics
 Birthrate- Number of LIVE births/1000 population
 Fertility rate- Annual number of births/1000 women between 
the ages of 15-44.
 Maternal mortality rate- number of maternal deaths from 
births and complications from pregnancy, childbirth and 
puerperium (42 days after the termination of a 
pregnancy)/100,000 births

Maternal-Infant Stats Cont.
 Infant mortality rate- number of deaths of infants under 1 yr 
of age/1000 live births
 Neonatal mortality rate- number of deaths of infants under 
28 days of age/1000 births
 Perinatal mortality rate- Number of stillbirths PLUS number 
of neonatal deaths/1000 births
 Stillbirths-An infant who demonstrates no signs of life- no 
breathing, heartbeat, or voluntary muscle movement.

CIA FactbookUS  
 173rd (of 227 nations) in infant mortality
 5.1/1000  vs. 1.5 in Slovenia
 122th (of 186 nations) in maternal mortality
  22/100,000 live births

Assessing the Community
 Access to health care
 Availability of health departments, hospitals, 
public clinics
 Poor accessibility because of geographic and 
transportation barriers
 Limitations of residing in rural areas or remote 
locations
 Cultural and language barriers
 Lack of providers in specialty care

10
Standards of Practice and Legal 
Issues
 Standards of practice in perinatal nursing
 American Nurses Association (ANA)
 AWHONN- Certification for L&D nurses
 American College of Nurse Midwives (ACNM)
 National Association of Neonatal Nurses (NANN) 
Certification for NICU nurses
 Risk management
 Sentinel events- “bad outcomes”
 Failure to Rescue- Neonatal as well as maternal

11
Ethical Issues in Perinatal Nursing 
 Reproductive technologies- political debate
 Substance Abuse- role of nurses in reporting
 Drug testing of infants
 Women seeking reproductive assistance
 95% of MDs would refuse HIV +
 61% would reject a single woman
 9% would reject women with less than a high-school diploma
(National Council on Disabilities)
 NYS requires HIV testing
 Mothers can refuse, however newborns will then be 
tested at birth
 Advances in care for the VLBW & premature
 Level III neonatal intensive care units
 Infants born before 26 weeks
 50% of preterm births have permanent impairment

Legal and Ethical Issues in 
Maternal and Women’s Health 
Care
 Abortion: legal, social, and political issue; 
nurses struggling with personal beliefs and 
professional duty 
 Substance abuse: fetal injury if woman is 
pregnant; possible charges of negligence and 
child endangerment
 Intrauterine therapy: medical technology vs. 
nature; better quality of life via surgical 
intervention

Stem Cell Research
 Goal is to relieve human suffering 
 Ethical concerns vary depending on the origin of 
the stem cells
 Controversy focuses on the use of embryonic 
stems cells
 Umbilical cord blood banking is a vast source of  
primitive hematopoietic stem and progenitor 
cells available for clinical application

RADAR
Domestic Partner Violence 
 R-routinely screen at every encounter
 Do you feel safe at home?
 Have you ever felt unsafe with your partner?
 A-Affirm feelings and Assess aburse
 D-Document your findings- notes, photos etc
 A-Assess for safety
 R-Review options and make referrals

Community-Based Nursing 
Care Settings
 Prenatal Care: Physicians’ office, hospital clinic, 
community free clinics, free-standing birth 
centers, home visits
 Childbirth Education: Private or community 
funded.  
 Breast-feeding education and support.
 Churches and shelters
 Client homes

Care Settings: Labor and Birth
 Hospital-Private OB/midwife model
 Women admitted to hospital 
 Evaluated by resident or RN-labor guidelines determine 
care
 OB generally present only close to birth 
 Midwifery model of care: midwife attends labor and birth
 Birthing center
 “Home-like” setting; close to hospital if complications; 
“normalcy” of birth- no epidural use
 Patient cared for by midwife or labor nurse 1:1 
 Home: Midwife 
 Family-centered birth; appropriate for women at low 
risk for complications, least expensive, limited 
availability to pain medication
 Midwives have collaborative agreement with MD if 
patient requires hospitalization
